definitions.definition: ut(x,t)=u_t(x,t)=d/dr u(x,r)|_{r=t}, the time partial derivative. Derivative notation uses the usual total derivative convention (zero if a derivative does not exist); no regularity property is granted by this definition.
utt(x,t)=u_tt(x,t)=d/dr ut(x,r)|_{r=t}, with the same total derivative convention.

definitions.type: family of maps ℝ^n×(0,∞)→ℝ^m indexed by j∈{1,…,n}
definitions.definition: dxu(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u(x,t), the partial derivative in the jth standard coordinate, with the total derivative convention. Further expressions ∂_{x_j}ut and ∂_{x_j}dxu(j,·,t) denote partial derivatives of the displayed functions; the latter is ∂_{x_jx_j}u.
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|²=|ut(x,t)|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|dxu(j,x,t)|². Norms are Euclidean; the sum is exactly the Frobenius square |D_xu|², with no factor 1/2.
et(x,t)=e_t(x,t)=d/dr e(x,r)|_{r=t}, with the total derivative convention. Its derivative and integral properties are proved, not part of the definition.

argument.text:
H002 gives continuous partial derivatives of every order on the open positive-time domain, so ut,utt,dxu are smooth. Squared Euclidean norms are finite sums of component squares, so e and its partial derivatives are smooth as well. Apply M009 at every (x,r) with r>0 to u (extended arbitrarily, say by q, outside the positive-time domain). Its C² germ is supplied by H002; over ℝ the threshold in M009 is 2. Evaluate symmetry on the time direction and each standard spatial coordinate direction to obtain ∂_r dxu(j,x,r)=∂_{x_j}ut(x,r). Apply M001 to the time sections ut with itself, and dxu(j) with itself, and add the finitely many resulting derivative formulas. The dot product is symmetric over ℝ, and |v|²=v·v, so for all x∈ℝ^n,r>0,
et(x,r)=2ut(x,r)·utt(x,r)+2Σ_{j=1}^n dxu(j,x,r)·∂_{x_j}ut(x,r).
This also proves smoothness of et. Each use of time sections on ℝ can use the extension by zero outside positive times, without changing their positive-time germs.

argument.text: Choose C from F002. Apply M010 to the identity map of Euclidean ℝ^n restricted to C. There exists a finite real bound on |x| for x∈C. Taking a positive number larger than that bound, for example one plus its maximum with zero, and using |x_j|≤|x|, gives existence of R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n. This argument also works when C is empty.

argument.text: Choose R from F003 and set Q=[-R,R]^n. H001 ensures the spatial dimension is a positive finite integer. The box is compact and has Lebesgue measure (2R)^n<∞. The compact set C is closed, so (ℝ^n\C)×int J is open; u equals the constant q there by F002. Every positive-order derivative of u is zero there: at each point its germ is constant, so the defining difference quotients, and then successively all derivative germs, are zero. Consequently at each r∈int J, e,et, ut·utt, dxu(j)·∂_{x_j}ut, ut·∂_{x_j}dxu(j), and ∂_{x_j}(ut·dxu(j)) vanish outside C, for every index j. H002 and F001 give continuity of these sections (products and finite sums of continuous derivative components). Their nonzero sets thus have closures contained in the closed compact C; hence they have compact support. M003 proves their absolute integrability. M010 on Q bounds each section; its absolute integral is bounded by its finite absolute bound times |Q| because it vanishes outside Q. In particular τ∈int J, so e(·,τ) is integrable. Since τ was arbitrary, this proves integrability at every positive time, together with all the asserted common-support and integrability statements and the global identities of F001.
